mappings.note: Predict and then record which wax-stuck pin falls first along the heated strip: an investigation with a prediction column and observations. The conduction explanation is drawn from it, but the recording is the task.
Tabulates observations about the cups together with probable reasons, again the conduct-and-record outcome.
The rising and falling streak of colour is explained as a convection current in heated water, which is a mode of heat transfer, named in LO-86.
Asks for the temperature rise of soil and of water over twenty minutes, which is reading and calculating from measured temperatures. LO-88 names temperature explicitly.
Predicts and compares how fast water seeps through clay, sand and gravel: a three-way comparison run as an experiment.
The saucepan body must conduct and the handle must not, so the item separates a conductor from an insulator of heat, the pairing LO-82 names.
Standing a leaking tumbler inside a second one traps air and keeps the lassi cold: insulation applied to an everyday fix. Not LO-82, because the materials are not being sorted.
True-or-false statements about conduction in solids, convection as bulk movement and the direction of a land breeze: all three are about the modes of heat transfer.
Where the melting ice gets its heat, namely from the surrounding air and the dish: the change traced to its source. Not LO-86, because no mode is being described in detail.
Smoke from a downward-pointing stick still rises by convection (LO-86), and the question explicitly asks for the movement to be drawn (LO-89).
Which thermometer reads higher turns on how heat spreads through water, hottest at the bottom near the flame. A mode-of-transfer explanation, so LO-86 rather than LO-88, since no measurement is made.
Hollow bricks in hot regions: trapped air used as insulation in real building practice.
Mild coastal temperatures traced to water heating and cooling slowly: a climatic phenomenon tied to its cause.
Describes rainwater seeping through soil and rock until it collects as groundwater: a process explained step by step.
Justifies the water cycle as redistributing and replenishing water through evaporation, condensation and precipitation: the whole process described.
Kerala's warmer, humid winter traced to its nearness to the equator and its coastline: climate related to its causes.
The Sun as the source of Earth's heat and light, the starting point of every transfer this chapter explains.
Metal cooking utensils because metals conduct heat well: the property behind an everyday object. The saucepan item that splits body from handle is on LO-82.
Defines conduction as transfer from hotter to colder part without particles moving: a mode of heat transfer.
How particles pass energy to neighbours while staying in place: the mechanism of conduction.
Names the good-conductors-of-heat class. Category naming, so LO-83 rather than LO-82, where two materials are set against each other.
Names the poor-conductor or insulator class, the companion category.
Wool keeps us warm because it traps air: insulation applied to clothing.
Two thin blankets beat one thick one because of the air layer between: the same insulation idea in another everyday case.
The one-mark version of the hollow-brick item, again trapped air used in construction.
The paper cup rises because the heated air below becomes lighter: an observed effect traced to its cause.
Smoke rises because hot gases are less dense than the surrounding air: the same cause-and-effect reasoning applied to a different sight.
Defines convection as transfer by the movement of the fluid itself.
Contrasts convection with conduction on whether particles move. The contrast is between two modes of transfer, not two materials, so LO-86 and not LO-82.
Soil heats faster than water: two materials separated by a thermal property, the differentiation LO-82 covers.
Soil also cools faster than water, the cooling half of the same material comparison.
Names the sea breeze and the daytime circulation that produces it: convection in the open air.
Windows facing the sea to catch the breeze is house design informed by the phenomenon, so the everyday-application outcome.
Names the land breeze and the night-time reversal of the same circulation.
Identifies both breezes as convection, which is placing a natural phenomenon under the right mode of transfer.
Radiation as the way heat reaches us with no contact and no air movement: the third mode of transfer.
Sorts the three modes by whether they need a medium, which rests on how each one works.
A hot utensil away from the flame cools because it radiates heat to its surroundings: the observed cooling traced to its cause.
Light clothes in summer because they reflect radiant heat: the concept applied to what we wear.
Dark clothes in winter because they absorb radiant heat, the winter counterpart of the same everyday choice.
